assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative-data research on intergenerational mobility has changed the measurement of opportunity and supplied an influential empirical framework for studying its geographic and policy correlates.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren, and Friedman form a clearly identifiable core for the linked mobility-data program; broader intellectual and data-system contributions remain relevant but do not obscure this attribution.
assessment.maturity: The research program is extensive, highly consequential, and has generated substantial follow-on work across public and labour economics.
uncertainties: The extent to which descriptive mobility patterns identify particular causal mechanisms remains contested.
The candidate framing combines measurement, data construction, and policy-relevant empirical analysis.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantile regression gave economics a durable way to study heterogeneous conditional outcomes rather than only conditional means, with exceptionally broad methodological and applied influence.
assessment.attribution: Koenker and Bassett are the central, tightly attributable originators of the core method; later distributional-method contributions should be distinguished from that original breakthrough.
assessment.maturity: The method has been established for decades, is widely used, and has supported a large theoretical and empirical literature.
uncertainties: The appropriate boundary between the foundational method and later advances in high-dimensional or semiparametric distributional analysis is not self-evident.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on tasks, technology, trade exposure, and local labour-market adjustment has reshaped understanding of changing labour demand and wage inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn, and Hanson are a coherent core for the empirical analysis of trade shocks and labour-market effects, while related work on technology and inequality has many important contributors.
assessment.maturity: The findings have been repeatedly studied, extended, and integrated into mainstream labour and trade research over a sustained period.
uncertainties: The candidate groups several mechanisms and research strands whose empirical magnitudes and welfare implications differ.
Attribution for the wider technology-and-inequality literature is necessarily broader than the proposed trio.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The integration of economic theory with credible measurement of selection in insurance markets has made a fundamental market-failure question empirically tractable and policy relevant.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are especially central to the modern empirical program; foundational adverse-selection theory and other empirical contributors require careful recognition.
assessment.maturity: This is a mature body of work with enduring influence in health, insurance, and public economics.
uncertainties: The contribution builds on a substantial earlier theoretical literature.
Evidence on selection and welfare can vary materially across institutional settings and insurance products.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Work on early-life conditions and skill formation has established childhood as a central economic source of later inequality, health, and human-capital differences.
assessment.attribution: Currie, Almond, and Cunha represent complementary empirical and conceptual contributions, though the underlying research program is wider than a single set of papers.
assessment.maturity: The area has accumulated extensive evidence and has strongly influenced research and policy discussion across health, education, and labour economics.
uncertainties: The candidate joins distinct approaches to early-life shocks, child health, and dynamic skill formation.
Long-run causal pathways are difficult to isolate fully.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The modern analysis of monopsony restored imperfect competition in labour markets to a central place in explaining wages, employer power, and labour-market policy.
assessment.attribution: Manning is a particularly clear intellectual focal point for the modern monopsony framework, even though the subsequent empirical literature has many contributors.
assessment.maturity: The framework has had lasting theoretical and empirical influence and has become central to contemporary labour-market analysis.
uncertainties: Measured labour-market power and the policy implications of particular estimates remain context dependent.
The candidate formulation spans both foundational theory and a broad subsequent empirical literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correspondence and audit-study evidence made discrimination in hiring observable in a transparent experimental framework and changed the empirical study of labour-market inequality.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are central to a landmark modern correspondence-study contribution; the broader audit tradition includes important preceding and subsequent work.
assessment.maturity: The design has been replicated and adapted widely, with enduring influence on research about discrimination and hiring.
uncertainties: Measured callback discrimination is not identical to discrimination over the full employment relationship.
External validity and the interpretation of experimental signals depend on the setting.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework offered a powerful quantitative account of how distorted input allocation across firms can affect productivity and income differences across countries.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh, Klenow, and Restuccia are closely associated with the central quantitative formulation and its development, while the underlying allocation and productivity traditions are broader.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been widely applied and remains a major reference point in growth and development research.
uncertainties: Inferring distortions from observed revenue productivity requires strong modeling and measurement assumptions.
The relative importance of misallocation compared with technology, institutions, and selection remains unsettled.
